subtopics.title: Key Facts, Matrices & Language Hierarchy
subtopics.subtitle: Language hierarchy, closure tables, automata tuples, transformation matrices and projections

concepts.text: Theory of computation questions test the language hierarchy, closure properties and the exact form of each automaton, lemma and normal form. Graphics questions test transformation matrices, clipping codes and projection types. This page puts all of them on one screen, in syllabus order, so you can rehearse them before a test.

concepts.plainText: DFA 5-tuple with δ: Q × Σ → Q; subset construction turns an n-state NFA into at most 2^n DFA states

items: DFA, NFA and ε-NFA recognise exactly the regular languages; NFAs are only more convenient, not more powerful.
Minimization merges indistinguishable states (partition / table-filling); the minimal DFA is unique up to renaming.
Regular expressions ↔ finite automata: Thompson's construction (RE → ε-NFA) and state elimination or Arden's theorem R = Q + RP ⇒ R = QP* (FA → RE).

concepts.latex: \text{Pumping (regular): } w = xyz,\ |xy| \le p,\ |y| \ge 1,\ xy^{i}z \in L\ \forall i \ge 0
concepts.plainText: Regular pumping lemma: w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1, and xy^i z in L for every i ≥ 0

concepts.latex: \text{CFG} = (V, T, P, S);\qquad \text{CNF: } A \to BC \mid a,\quad |w| = n \Rightarrow 2n - 1 \text{ steps}
concepts.plainText: CFG 4-tuple; Chomsky normal form A → BC | a, a string of length n takes 2n − 1 derivation steps

items: A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees (equivalently two leftmost derivations); E → E + E | E * E | id is the classic example.
GNF: every production is A → aα; BNF writes rules as <expr> ::= <expr> + <term> | <term>.
PDA = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F); acceptance by final state and by empty stack are equivalent for NPDAs; DPDAs are weaker (they cannot accept even-length palindromes).
CFG ↔ PDA: every CFL has an NPDA and every NPDA's language is context-free.

concepts.plainText: CFL pumping lemma: w = uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1, uv^i w x^i y in L for every i ≥ 0

concepts.latex: \text{TM} = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, B, F),\qquad \delta: Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L, R\}
concepts.plainText: TM 7-tuple with δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}

items: Recursive (decidable) languages have a TM that always halts; recursively enumerable ones have a TM that halts on every member but may loop otherwise.
Multi-track, multi-tape, two-way-infinite and non-deterministic TMs all recognise the same languages as a standard TM (only speed differs).
A universal TM takes an encoded machine ⟨M⟩ and input w and simulates M on w.
Church–Turing thesis: every effectively computable function is Turing-computable.
Undecidable: halting problem, Post correspondence problem, CFG ambiguity and equivalence; Rice's theorem covers every non-trivial property of RE languages.

rows: a solution can be verified in polynomial time
in NP and every NP problem reduces to it
at least as hard as NP-complete; may not be in NP

concepts.plainText: Frame-buffer size = resolution × bit depth; n bits per pixel give 2^n colours

rows: whole screen refreshed line by line from a frame buffer
only the lines in the display file are drawn
flicker with complex scenes; no area fill

items: Refresh rate ≥ 60 Hz avoids flicker; interlacing draws odd then even lines.
The video controller reads the frame buffer; a display processor (graphics controller, GPU) does scan conversion and raster operations.
Logical input classes: locator, stroke, string, valuator, choice, pick (light pen is the classic pick device).
Standards: GKS (first ISO standard, 2D), PHIGS (3D, hierarchical), CGM (metafile), OpenGL (open, cross-platform), DirectX (Windows).

concepts.plainText: Translation: x' = x + t_x, y' = y + t_y (3 × 3 homogeneous matrix)
Rotation: x' = x cos θ − y sin θ, y' = x sin θ + y cos θ

concepts.latex: S = \begin{bmatrix} s_x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\qquad \text{shear: } x' = x + sh_x\,y
concepts.plainText: 2D scaling matrix; x-shear moves x by sh_x times y
Rotation about a pivot: translate pivot to origin, rotate, translate back (applied right to left)
Window-to-viewport mapping for x (same form for y)

items: Cohen–Sutherland region code bits TBRL (top, bottom, right, left); inside = 0000.
Both codes 0000 → trivially accept; bitwise AND ≠ 0000 → trivially reject; otherwise clip against an edge and repeat.
Liang–Barsky uses x = x1 + tΔx with p1 = −Δx, p2 = Δx, p3 = −Δy, p4 = Δy and q_k from the window; t = q_k/p_k, entering when p_k < 0, leaving when p_k > 0; fewer intersections than Cohen–Sutherland.

concepts.latex: R_z(\theta):\ x' = x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta,\ y' = x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta,\ z' = z
concepts.plainText: Rotation about z in 3D; rotations about x and y follow by cycling x → y → z → x

items: 3D homogeneous coordinates use 4 × 4 matrices on (x, y, z, 1).
Reflection about the xy-plane negates z; about yz negates x; about xz negates y.
Rotation about an arbitrary axis: translate the axis through the origin, rotate it onto the z-axis, rotate by θ, then undo the alignment and the translation in reverse order.
Viewing pipeline: modelling → world → viewing (camera: VRP, view-plane normal N, view-up V) → projection → normalised → clipping → device.

receding lines at 45° with L = 1 / L = 1/2
cavalier keeps depth length, cabinet halves it
x_p = x d / z, y_p = y d / z

notes.text: Closure questions are the easiest marks in this chapter: regular languages are closed under everything listed; context-free languages fail only intersection and complement; recursively enumerable languages fail only complement.
Matrix order: with column vectors the rightmost matrix is applied first, so T(p)·R(θ)·T(−p) translates to the origin first. Swapping the order gives a rotation about the wrong point.
Remember the machine for each language class as a ladder: FA (no memory) < PDA (one stack) < LBA (bounded tape) < TM (unbounded tape). Adding a second stack to a PDA already gives Turing power.

formulas.title: Subset-construction bound
formulas.description: Each DFA state is a subset of NFA states; usually far fewer are reachable.

formulas.title: Regular pumping lemma
formulas.plainText: w = xyz, |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1, xy^i z ∈ L for all i ≥ 0
formulas.description: Used to prove a language is NOT regular by showing some pumped string leaves L.

formulas.title: 2D rotation
formulas.latex: x' = x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta,\qquad y' = x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta
formulas.plainText: x' = x cos θ − y sin θ;  y' = x sin θ + y cos θ
formulas.description: Anticlockwise rotation about the origin by θ.

formulas.title: Window-to-viewport
formulas.latex: x_v = xv_{min} + (x_w - xw_{min})\,s_x,\quad s_x = \frac{xv_{max} - xv_{min}}{xw_{max} - xw_{min}}
formulas.description: The same form maps y; unequal s_x and s_y distort the aspect ratio.

formulas.title: Perspective projection
formulas.description: Centre of projection at the origin, view plane at z = d; farther points shrink.

flashcards.front: Under which operations are context-free languages NOT closed?
flashcards.back: Intersection and complement (they are closed under union, concatenation, star, homomorphism and intersection with a regular language).

flashcards.front: Give the Cohen–Sutherland trivial accept and trivial reject tests.
flashcards.back: Accept if both endpoint codes are 0000; reject if the bitwise AND of the two codes is not 0000.

flashcards.front: What is the composite matrix for scaling about a fixed point (x_f, y_f)?
flashcards.back: T(x_f, y_f) · S(s_x, s_y) · T(−x_f, −y_f): move the point to the origin, scale, move back.

questions.questionText: Which of the following languages is context-free but NOT regular?
questions.explanation: aⁿbⁿ needs one counter, which a PDA's stack provides but no finite automaton can; aⁿbⁿcⁿ and ww are not context-free, and (a + b)* is regular.

questions.questionText: The point (3, 4) is rotated by 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Its new coordinates are:
questions.explanation: x' = x cos 90° − y sin 90° = −4 and y' = x sin 90° + y cos 90° = 3.

questions.questionText: A screen of 1280 × 1024 pixels with 8 bits per pixel needs a frame buffer of:
Which statement about Turing machine variants is correct?
options: A multi-tape TM can recognise languages a single-tape TM cannot
A non-deterministic TM recognises exactly the same languages as a deterministic TM
A two-stack PDA is strictly weaker than a TM
A TM with a read-only tape is as powerful as a standard TM
questions.explanation: All standard variants (multi-tape, multi-track, non-deterministic) have the same power; a two-stack PDA equals a TM, and a read-only tape reduces the machine to a finite automaton.
